# From Equations to Systems

- [Three tiny equations](#three-tiny-equations)
- [From one equation to systems of equations](#from-one-equation-to-systems-of-equations)
- [Three systems, three solution sets](#three-systems-three-solution-sets)
- [The solution is where the lines meet](#the-solution-is-where-the-lines-meet)
- [Solve by manipulating the equations while preserving the solution set](#solve-by-manipulating-the-equations-while-preserving-the-solution-set)
- [Three reversible moves](#three-reversible-moves)
- [Reversible—or not?](#reversibleor-not)


## Three tiny equations

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
$$
2x=-1
$$

[One]{.alert} solution

$$x=-\tfrac12$$
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
$$
0x=-1
$$

[No]{.alert} solutions

$$0=-1$$
:::

::: {.column width="34%"}
$$
0x=0
$$

[$\infty$ many]{.alert} solutions

$$x\text{ arbitrary}$$
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
We transform equations in ways that are [reversible]{.alert} and so preserve the solution set
:::

For the second and third examples, no reversible transformation can isolate $x$: a zero coefficient remains zero

::: {.key-point}
A system of $m$ linear equations in $n$ unknowns has exactly one of three outcomes:

- one solution
- no solutions
- infinitely many solutions
:::

## From one equation to systems of equations

- A [solution]{.alert} makes every equation true at once
- A [solution set]{.alert} contains all such choices of the unknowns
- First tool: [reversible]{.alert} transformations of equations

::: {.key-point}
Solve a system by replacing it with an easier system having exactly the same solutions
:::

## Three systems, three solution sets

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
\begin{align*}
x+y&=3\\
3x-y&=5
\end{align*}

Exactly one

$$\{(2,1)\}$$
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
\begin{align*}
x+y&=3\\
x+y&=4
\end{align*}

None

$$\varnothing$$
:::

::: {.column width="34%"}
\begin{align*}
x+y&=3\\
2x+2y&=6
\end{align*}

Infinitely many

$$\{(3-t,t):t\in\reals\}$$
:::
:::

$\exstar$ What relationship between the two equations produces each outcome?

## Solve by manipulating the equations while preserving the solution set

Suppose $(x,y)$ satisfies

\begin{align*}
x+y&=3  &(E_1)\\
3x-y&=5 & (E_2)
\end{align*}

Then it also satisfies

\begin{align*}
x+y&=3  &(E_1)\\
-4y&=-4 & (E_2)-3 (E_1)
\end{align*}

And the original system of equations can be recovered because

$$E_2 = \bigl(E_2-3(E_1) \bigr) +3E_1=E_2$$

::: {.key-point}
The new system contains the same information because the step can be undone, i.e., it is reversible
:::

## Three reversible moves

| Transformation of the equations | Inverse transformation |
|---|---|
| Interchange $E_i$ and $E_j$ | interchange them again |
| Replace $E_i$ by $E_i+cE_j$ | replace it by $E_i-cE_j$ |
| Replace $E_i$ by $cE_i$, $c\ne0$ | multiply by $1/c$ |

::: {.key-point}
These [elementary row operations]{.alert} preserve the entire solution set
:::

- The restriction $c\ne0$ for the last move matters: multiplying an equation by $0$ discards information

- The last move is not really needed

## Reversible—or not?

$\exstar$ Decide whether each transformation preserves the solution set for every system

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
1. $E_3\leftarrow 0E_3$

2. $E_1\leftrightarrow E_3$

3. $E_2\leftarrow E_2-2E_1$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
4. $E_2\leftarrow E_1+E_2$, then discard $E_1$

5. $E_1\leftarrow -3E_1$

6. $E_1 \leftarrow E_1^2$
:::
:::

For each reversible step, name its inverse

# Eliminate on Equations

- [Elimination](#elimination)
- [Back substitution](#back-substitution)
- [Why elimination works](#why-elimination-works)

We will return to one system throughout the lecture:

\begin{align*}
x+2y-z&=2 \qquad &(E_1)\\
2x-y+z&=-3 &(E_2)\\
3x+y+2z&=1 &(E_3)
\end{align*}

Goal: create equations with fewer unknowns while preserving every solution

## Elimination

### Eliminate $x$ in the equations below the first

Keep $E_1$ and use it to remove $x$ from the equations below:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x+2y-z&=2\\
2x-y+z&=-3\\
3x+y+2z&=1
\end{aligned}
\quad
\xrightarrow[\ E_3\leftarrow E_3-3E_1\ ]{\ E_2\leftarrow E_2-2E_1\ }
\quad
\begin{aligned}
x+2y-z&=2\\
-5y+3z&=-7\\
-5y+5z&=-5
\end{aligned}
$$

Each arrow abbreviates a reversible transformation

$$
E_2^{\mathrm{old}}=E_2^{\mathrm{new}}+2E_1,
\qquad
E_3^{\mathrm{old}}=E_3^{\mathrm{new}}+3E_1
$$

---

### Eliminate $y$ in the equations below the second
$$
\begin{aligned}
x+2y-z&=2\\
-5y+3z&=-7\\
-5y+5z&=-5
\end{aligned}
\quad
\xrightarrow{\ E_3\leftarrow E_3-E_2\ }
\quad
\begin{aligned}
x+2y-z&=2\\
-5y+3z&=-7\\
2z&=2
\end{aligned}
$$

## Back substitution

\begin{align*}
2z&=2 & \implies z& = \frac{2}{2} = 1 \\
-5y+3z& =-7 &\implies y &= \frac{-7 - 3\times 1}{-5} = 2 \\
x+2y-z & =2 & \implies x & = 2 - (2\times 2 - 1)=-1
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
The original system has the unique solution $(x,y,z)=(-1,2,1)$
:::

## Why elimination works

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
1. Eliminate $x$ below the first equation

   $\implies$ an equivalent system

2. Eliminate $y$ below the second equation

   $\implies$ an equivalent triangular system

3. Back substitution reveals the solution
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
Elimination [does not]{.alert}

- guess a solution
- approximate the equations
- change the constraints

Elimination [does]{.alert} expose information already present
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
Each system at each step has [exactly the same solution set]{.alert} because every elimination step is [reversible]{.alert}
:::

# The Dot Product

The dot product connects algebraic computation with geometric length, angle, and orthogonality

- [What the dot product reveals](#what-the-dot-product-reveals)
- [A linear equation describes a hyperplane](#a-linear-equation-describes-a-hyperplane)
- [Each equation is one dot product](#each-equation-is-one-dot-product)
- [Matrix–matrix multiplication collects dot products](#matrix-matrix-multiplication-collects-dot-products)
- [A general linear system](#a-general-linear-system)

## What the dot product reveals

### Combines coefficients and unknowns

For $\vct{a},\vct{x}\in\reals^n$, the [dot product]{.alert}

$$
\vct{a}^{\top}\vct{x}
=a_1x_1+\cdots+a_nx_n
$$

Example:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 & 3\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{bmatrix}
=2x-y+3z
$$

::: {.key-point}
A [dot product]{.alert} turns two vectors into one scalar by pairing corresponding entries

&nbsp;

The standard dot product on $\reals^n$ is our first [inner product]{.alert}—the model for measuring length, angle, and orthogonality
:::

---

### Measures alignment

For nonzero $\vct{a},\vct{x}\in\reals^n$, let $\theta\in[0,\pi]$ be the angle between them

The dot product defines the [Euclidean norm]{.alert} and measures alignment:

\begin{align*}
\lVert\vct{a}\rVert
  &= \sqrt{\vct{a}^{\top}\vct{a}}
   = \sqrt{a_1^2+\cdots+a_n^2},\\
\vct{a}^{\top}\vct{x}
  &= \lVert\vct{a}\rVert\,\lVert\vct{x}\rVert\cos(\theta).
\end{align*}

- $\vct{a}^{\top}\vct{x}>0$ — acute angle
- $\vct{a}^{\top}\vct{x}=0$ — right angle
- $\vct{a}^{\top}\vct{x}<0$ — obtuse angle

::: {.key-point}
Two vectors are [orthogonal]{.alert} when $\vct{a}^{\top}\vct{x}=0$

&nbsp;

Nonzero orthogonal vectors are perpendicular
:::

---

### Why the cosine appears

The three points $\vct{0},\vct{a},\vct{x}$ lie in a plane or along a line.

<svg class="diagram-image dot-product-cosine-geometry" viewBox="0 0 700 390" width="68%" role="img" aria-label="A plane contains the triangle with vertices zero, a, and x.  Arrows from zero to a and zero to x form the angle theta.  The arrow from x to a is a minus x.">

---

### Geometry meets coordinate algebra

The planar [Law of Cosines]{.alert} gives

$$
\lVert\vct{a}-\vct{x}\rVert^2
=\lVert\vct{a}\rVert^2+\lVert\vct{x}\rVert^2
-2\lVert\vct{a}\rVert\lVert\vct{x}\rVert\cos(\theta)
$$

Coordinate algebra gives

\begin{align*}
\lVert\vct{a}-\vct{x}\rVert^2
  &=(\vct{a}-\vct{x})^{\top}(\vct{a}-\vct{x})\\
  &=\lVert\vct{a}\rVert^2+\lVert\vct{x}\rVert^2
    -2\vct{a}^{\top}\vct{x}
\end{align*}

Comparing the two expressions proves

$$
\vct{a}^{\top}\vct{x}
=\lVert\vct{a}\rVert\lVert\vct{x}\rVert\cos(\theta)
$$

::: {.key-point}
In $\reals^n$, geometry explains the formula; in a general inner-product space, the formula [defines the angle]{.alert}
:::

---

### Parallel vectors point along one line

Nonzero vectors $\vct{a}$ and $\vct{x}$ are [parallel]{.alert} when

$$
\vct{x}=\lambda\vct{a}
\qquad\text{for some }\lambda\ne0
$$

- $\lambda>0$ — same direction
- $\lambda<0$ — opposite directions
- angle $0$ or $\pi$
- $\vct{a}^{\top}\vct{x}
  = \pm \lVert\vct{a}\rVert\,\lVert\vct{x}\rVert$

::: {.key-point}
Parallel vectors are nonzero scalar multiples of one another
:::

## A linear equation describes a hyperplane

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="53%"}
For nonzero $\vct{a}\in\reals^n$, let $\vct{x}$ range over $\reals^n$. The solution set

$$
H=\{\vct{x}\in\reals^n:\vct{a}^{\top}\vct{x}=b\}
$$

is an $(n-1)$-dimensional [hyperplane]{.alert} with normal vector $\vct{a}$

Choose two particular points $\vct{u},\vct{t}\in H$. Then

$$
\vct{a}^{\top}(\vct{u}-\vct{t})
=\vct{a}^{\top}\vct{u}-\vct{a}^{\top}\vct{t}
=b-b=0
$$
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}

:::

### Parallel equations with two possible outcomes

$$
\va_1^\top \vx = b_1 \qquad \va_2^\top \vx = b_2
$$

Suppose $\vct{a}_2=\lambda\vct{a}_1$ with $\lambda\ne0$

- Left sides point in the same normal direction
- Right sides decide whether the planes coincide

## Each equation is one dot product

Write each matrix row as the transpose of a coefficient vector:

\begin{align*}
\begin{matrix}
x + 2y -z = 2 \\
2x - y + z = -3 \\
3x + y + 2z = 1
\end{matrix}
\iff
\begin{matrix}
\vct{a}_1^{\top}\vct{x}=2
&\vct{a}_1^{\top}=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&-1\end{bmatrix}\\
\vct{a}_2^{\top}\vct{x}=-3
&\vct{a}_2^{\top}=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1&1\end{bmatrix}\\
\vct{a}_3^{\top}\vct{x}=1
&\vct{a}_3^{\top}=\begin{bmatrix}3&1&2\end{bmatrix}
\end{matrix}
\quad
\vct{x}=\begin{bmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{bmatrix}
\end{align*}

Stack the coefficient rows to get

$$
\mA \vx = \vb
$$

where

$$
\mat{A}=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&2&-1\\
2&-1&1\\
3&1&2
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\vct{b}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\-3\\1\end{bmatrix}
$$

---

### What $\mat{A}\vct{x}$ means

$$
\mat{A}\vct{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\vct{a}_1^{\top}\vct{x}\\
\vct{a}_2^{\top}\vct{x}\\
\vdots\\
\vct{a}_m^{\top}\vct{x}
\end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\vct{a}_i^{\top}=\text{row }i\text{ of }\mat{A}
$$

Thus

$$
\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\vct{a}_i^{\top}\vct{x}=b_i
\quad(i=1,\ldots,m)
$$

::: {.key-point}
[Matrix–vector multiplication]{.alert}: every matrix row takes a dot product with the vector
:::

## Matrix–matrix multiplication collects dot products {#matrix-matrix-multiplication-collects-dot-products}

For $\mat{A}\in\reals^{m\times n}$, use uppercase vector symbols for columns and lowercase vector symbols for rows

\begin{gather*}
\mat{A}=[\vct{A}_1,\ldots,\vct{A}_n]
\qquad
\mat{A}=\begin{bmatrix}\vct{a}_1^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ \vct{a}_m^{\top}\end{bmatrix}
\end{gather*}

and likewise for $\mat{B}\in\reals^{n\times p}$ and $\mat{C}=\mat{A}\mat{B}\in\reals^{m\times p}$

### By columns

\begin{align*}
 [\vct{C}_1,\ldots,\vct{C}_p]
  = \mat{C}
  = \mat{A}\mat{B}
  &= \mat{A}[\vct{B}_1,\ldots,\vct{B}_p]
   = [\mat{A}\vct{B}_1,\ldots,\mat{A}\vct{B}_p]
\end{align*}

---

### By rows

\begin{align*}
\begin{bmatrix}\vct{c}_1^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ \vct{c}_m^{\top}\end{bmatrix}
  = \mat{C}
  = \mat{A}\mat{B}
  &= \begin{bmatrix}\vct{a}_1^{\top}\\ \vdots\\ \vct{a}_m^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\mat{B}
   = \begin{bmatrix}\vct{a}_1^{\top}\mat{B}\\ \vdots\\ \vct{a}_m^{\top}\mat{B}\end{bmatrix}
\end{align*}

### Entrywise

\begin{align*}
\begin{bmatrix}c_{11}&\cdots&c_{1p}\\ \vdots&&\vdots\\ c_{m1}&\cdots&c_{mp}\end{bmatrix}
  = \mat{C}
  = \mat{A}\mat{B}
  &= \begin{bmatrix}
       \vct{a}_1^{\top}\vct{B}_1 & \cdots & \vct{a}_1^{\top}\vct{B}_p\\
       \vdots & & \vdots\\
       \vct{a}_m^{\top}\vct{B}_1 & \cdots & \vct{a}_m^{\top}\vct{B}_p
     \end{bmatrix}
\end{align*}

::: {.key-point}
[Matrix–matrix multiplication]{.alert} collects all dot products of rows of the first matrix with columns of the second.

&nbsp;

It is [associative but generally not commutative]{.alert}: compatible factors may be regrouped, not reordered.
:::

## A general linear system

\begin{align*}
a_{11}x_1+\cdots+a_{1n}x_n&=b_1\\
&\ \vdots\\
a_{m1}x_1+\cdots+a_{mn}x_n&=b_m
\end{align*}

becomes

$$
\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b},
\qquad
\mat{A}\in\reals^{m\times n},
\quad
\vct{x}\in\reals^n,
\quad
\vct{b}\in\reals^m
$$

The compact notation records all $m$ equations at once

---

### The augmented matrix stores the system

$$
\left.
\begin{aligned}
x+2y-z&=2\\
2x-y+z&=-3\\
3x+y+2z&=1
\end{aligned}
\quad\right\}
\qquad\longleftrightarrow\qquad
\left[\mat{A}\mid\vct{b}\right]
=
\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|r}
1&2&-1&2\\
2&-1&1&-3\\
3&1&2&1
\end{array}
\right]
$$

- variable order fixed: $x,y,z$
- vertical bar separates coefficients from right-hand sides
- each matrix row represents one equation

::: {.key-point}
Row operations on $[\mat{A}\mid\vct{b}]$ are compact versions of reversible operations on the equations
:::

# Eliminate on Matrices

[Compute with rows first]{.alert}; reinterpret the same steps as reversible matrix actions later

- [Translate equations into matrix rows](#translate-equations-into-matrix-rows)
- [Eliminate and organize with pivots](#eliminate-and-organize-with-pivots)
- [Read the solution set (back substitution)](#read-the-solution-set)
- [Resistance circuit](#resistance-circuit)
- [Row operations are reversible matrix actions](#row-operations-are-reversible-matrix-actions)

## Translate equations into matrix rows

### One step, two notations

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
#### Operate on equations

Start with

$$
\begin{aligned}
x+2y-z&=2 &&(E_1)\\
2x-y+z&=-3 &&(E_2)\\
3x+y+2z&=1 &&(E_3)
\end{aligned}
$$

Apply $E_2\leftarrow E_2-2E_1$:

$$
-5y+3z=-7
$$
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
#### Operate on rows

The same coefficients and right-hand sides give

$$
\begin{gathered}
\left[\begin{array}{rrr|r}
1&2&-1&2\\2&-1&1&-3\\3&1&2&1
\end{array}\right]
\\[-0.2em]
\overset{R_2\leftarrow R_2-2R_1}{\Downarrow}
\\[-0.2em]
\left[\begin{array}{rrr|r}
1&2&-1&2\\0&-5&3&-7\\3&1&2&1
\end{array}\right]
\end{gathered}
$$
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
$E_i$ names an equation; $R_i$ names the corresponding matrix row
:::

## Eliminate and organize with pivots

For a solve, operate directly on $[\,\mat{A}\mid\vct{b}\,]$; this is closest to the computation carried out by software

### Matrix elimination repeats the same work

Continue the same elimination with compact matrix notation:

\begin{align*}
&\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|r}
1&2&-1&2\\2&-1&1&-3\\3&1&2&1
\end{array}
\right]
\xrightarrow[\ R_3\leftarrow R_3-3R_1\ ]{\ R_2\leftarrow R_2-2R_1\ }
\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|r}
1&2&-1&2\\0&-5&3&-7\\0&-5&5&-5
\end{array}
\right]\\[0.8em]
&\hspace{7em}\xrightarrow{\ R_3\leftarrow R_3-R_2\ }
\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|r}
1&2&-1&2\\0&-5&3&-7\\0&0&2&2
\end{array}
\right]
\end{align*}

---

### Pivots organize elimination

$$
\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|r}
\alert{1}&2&-1&2\\
0&\alert{-5}&3&-7\\
0&0&\alert{2}&2
\end{array}
\right]
$$

- [pivot]{.alert} — leading nonzero entry in a nonzero row
- entries below each pivot are zero
- each pivot lies to the right of the pivot above it
- zero rows, if any, lie at the bottom

This is [row echelon form]{.alert}

::: {.small}
Pivot entries need not equal $1$ in row echelon form
:::

---

### A zero pivot candidate requires a row exchange

The first entry cannot serve as a pivot

\begin{align*}
\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|r}
0&1&1&3\\
1&1&-1&0\\
2&-1&1&3
\end{array}
\right]
&\xrightarrow{\ R_1\leftrightarrow R_2\ }
\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|r}
1&1&-1&0\\
0&1&1&3\\
2&-1&1&3
\end{array}
\right]
\end{align*}

Now the entry in position $(1,1)$ can organize elimination below it

::: {.key-point}
When a pivot candidate is zero, exchange rows to bring a nonzero entry into the pivot position
:::

$\exstar$ After the exchange, which row operation eliminates the $2$ below the new first pivot?

## Read the solution set (back substitution) {#read-the-solution-set}

### Read the unique solution by back substitution

\begin{align*}
\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|r}
1&2&-1&2\\0&-5&3&-7\\0&0&2&2
\end{array}
\right]
&\qquad\longleftrightarrow\qquad
\begin{aligned}
x+2y-z&=2\\
-5y+3z&=-7\\
2z&=2
\end{aligned}\\
&\qquad\implies\qquad
z=1,\quad y=2,\quad x=-1
\end{align*}

Every variable column contains a pivot

::: {.key-point}
No variable can be chosen freely, so the consistent system has exactly one solution
:::

---

### The bottom row(s) reveal the other possibilities

Suppose elimination instead produced one of these echelon forms

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
#### Contradiction

$$
\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|r}
1&2&-1&2\\
0&-5&3&-7\\
0&0&0&2
\end{array}
\right]
$$

A bottom row represents the equation $0=2$

[Inconsistent]{.alert} — no solutions
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
#### Missing constraint

$$
\left[
\begin{array}{rrr|r}
1&2&-1&2\\
0&-5&3&-7\\
0&0&0&0
\end{array}
\right]
$$

A bottom row represents the equation $0=0$

[Consistent]{.alert}, but one variable has no pivot
:::
:::

---

### Reverse the row operations to recover three planes

Undoing the same elimination steps gives two possible original systems

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
#### Contradiction

\begin{align*}
x+2y-z&=2\\
2x-y+z&=-3\\
3x+y&=1
\end{align*}

The first two equations imply $3x+y=-1$, which conflicts with the third
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}

:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
#### Missing constraint

\begin{align*}
x+2y-z&=2\\
2x-y+z&=-3\\
3x+y&=-1
\end{align*}

The third equation is the sum of the first two
:::
:::

::: {.key-point}
Reversible row operations let us move between the original planes and the bottom-row evidence
:::

---

### Geometry reveals the solution set

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
#### No common intersection

:::

---

### A free variable produces infinitely many solutions

For the consistent echelon system

\begin{align*}
x+2y-z&=2\\
-5y+3z&=-7\\
0&=0,
\end{align*}

The $z$ column has no pivot, so $z$ is the [free variable]{.alert}:

$$
y=\frac{7+3z}{5},
\qquad
x=\frac{-4-z}{5}
$$

$$
\left\{
\left(\frac{-4-z}{5},\frac{7+3z}{5},z\right):z\in\reals
\right\}
$$

Different values of $z$ give infinitely many solutions

---

### Now the three outcomes are visible

After elimination:

| Row structure | What it means | Number of solutions |
|---|---|---|
| $[\,0\ \cdots\ 0\mid c\,]$, $c\ne0$ | contradiction | none |
| consistent; pivot in every variable column | every variable determined | exactly one |
| consistent; fewer pivots than variables | one or more parameters | infinitely many |

::: {.key-point}
A linear system has zero, one, or infinitely many solutions—never exactly two
:::

$\exstar$ Why would two distinct solutions force infinitely many?

## Row operations are reversible matrix actions

Matrix multiplication gives an [algebraic representation]{.alert} of the same row operations in the language of vectors and matrices

### The same step is left multiplication

The $3\times3$ [identity matrix]{.alert} has ones on its diagonal and zeros elsewhere:

$$
\mat{I}=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1
\end{bmatrix}
\xrightarrow{R_2\leftarrow R_2-2R_1}
\mat{M}_1=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\-2&1&0\\0&0&1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Then [left multiplication]{.alert} performs that row operation:

$$
\mat{M}_1[\,\mat{A}\mid\vct{b}\,]
=
\left[\begin{array}{rrr|r}
1&2&-1&2\\0&-5&3&-7\\3&1&2&1
\end{array}\right]
$$

::: {.key-point}
$\mat{M}_1$ is an [elementary matrix]{.alert}: equation operation, row operation, and matrix multiplication describe the same step
:::

---

### Try it: connect the three views

$\exstar$ Return to the operation that eliminated $x$ from equation $E_3$:

$$
E_3\leftarrow E_3-3E_1
$$

1. Write the corresponding operation on row $R_3$
2. Build $\mat{M}_2$ by applying that row operation to $\mat{I}$
3. Verify that $\mat{M}_2[\,\mat{A}\mid\vct{b}\,]$ produces the same augmented matrix

::: {.key-point}
Before computing: which rows must remain unchanged?
:::

---

### Undoing restores the original system

Undo $R_2\leftarrow R_2-2R_1$ with $R_2\leftarrow R_2+2R_1$:

$$
\mat{N}_1=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\2&1&0\\0&0&1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Indeed,

$$
\mat{N}_1\mat{M}_1=\mat{I}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Associativity shows that the whole system is restored:

$$
\mat{N}_1\bigl(\mat{M}_1[\,\mat{A}\mid\vct{b}\,]\bigr)
=(\mat{N}_1\mat{M}_1)[\,\mat{A}\mid\vct{b}\,]
=[\,\mat{A}\mid\vct{b}\,]
$$

::: {.key-point}
[Inverses]({{< meta decks.d02.file >}}) will call $\mat{N}_1$ the [inverse]{.alert} of $\mat{M}_1$
:::

---

### Elimination is an ordered product

If elimination applies $\mat{M}_1,\ldots,\mat{M}_k$, then

$$
\mat{M}_k\cdots\mat{M}_1
[\,\mat{A}\mid\vct{b}\,]
=
[\,\mat{U}\mid\vct{c}\,]
$$

This product records the elimination algebraically; it [need not be formed]{.alert} to solve the system

- the [rightmost matrix]{.alert} $\mat{M}_1$ acts first

::: {.key-point}
Matrix multiplication is [associative]{.alert}: factors may be regrouped. It is generally [not commutative]{.alert}: factors may not be reordered.
:::

# Big Ideas {data-state="goldborder"}

- [Equations show the details]{.alert}; [augmented matrices compress the same information]{.alert} for computation; [elementary matrices encode row operations algebraically]{.alert}
- Reversible row operations preserve the solution set
- Dot products express individual equations; matrix multiplication collects many dot products and composes actions
- Pivots organize elimination and reveal whether a system has [zero, one, or infinitely many solutions]{.alert}
- Compute only what the problem requires: direct elimination solves the system; elementary-matrix products record the process but need not be formed

Use computation to carry out row operations—not to replace interpretation

## Companion computation

[Lecture 01 companion notebook](https://github.com/fjhickernell/MATH332Fall2026/blob/main/notebooks/demonstrations/01-systems-and-matrices.ipynb){.alert} — executable working draft

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
Companion notebook workflow

- predict before computing
- trace exact elimination and back substitution with SymPy
- classify all three solution outcomes
- solve unique systems numerically with NumPy
- interpret exact and numerical residuals
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
from sympy import Matrix

A = Matrix([[1, 2, -1],
            [2, -1, 1],
            [3, 1, 2]])
b = Matrix([2, -3, 1])
A.row_join(b).echelon_form()
np.linalg.solve(np.array(A, dtype=float),
                np.array(b, dtype=float).ravel())
```

Standard kernel: `qmcpy`
:::
:::

## Where this leads

Elimination answers a concrete question:

$$
\text{Which }\vct{x}\text{ satisfy }\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}\text{?}
$$

It also opens structural questions:

- Which right-hand sides $\vct{b}$ are attainable?
- When does $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ have a unique solution for every $\vct{b}$?
- What do pivots tell us about the rows and columns of $\mat{A}$?
- How does algebra reveal the geometry of the solution set?
